fable-5.1.text:
I think it is one possible equilibrium. I'm not sure it's the only one, but it's one that I can actually imagine being stable.

The thing is, if you have AIs that are vastly more capable than people, then the question becomes, what are people doing in that world? You could have a world where the AIs are aligned, they care about people, and people are kind of... sitting there. They're taken care of, but they don't understand what's going on. And I think a lot of people, when they imagine that world, they find it unsatisfying. Something feels off about it.

So then the idea of people becoming part-AI, some kind of Neuralink++, is a way to address that. If you can actually understand what's happening, if you can participate, then you're not just a passive recipient of whatever the AI decides. You're part of the thing. And I think there is something appealing about that, because then it's less about whether the AI will be nice to you and more about whether you are one of the entities that gets to decide.

Now, I'll be honest, it's hard to think about this clearly. You're talking about a future that's quite different from anything we've experienced. So I hold it loosely. But if you ask me, what does a world look like where humanity is still relevant after superintelligence, I think the honest answer is that in the long run, there's a good chance that it involves people changing. Not necessarily all people, and not all at once, but that this is where the equilibrium is. The alternative, where there's a permanent gap in understanding between humans and AIs, I find harder to picture as something that stays stable for a very long time.

opus-5.5.text:
So, I'll say upfront that I don't love this answer, but I think it is an answer, and that's something.

Here's the problem it addresses. Suppose things go well in the near term, and every person has an AI that works on their behalf. It earns money for them, advocates for them in politics, writes the reports. The person reads the report and says, "Great, keep it up." It sounds nice, but the person is no longer a participant. They are a spectator. The AIs are the ones doing things and understanding things, and the human is along for the ride. I think that's a precarious equilibrium, maybe not an equilibrium at all, because there's no real reason for it to stay that way.

Now imagine instead that people become part AI, with some kind of Neuralink++. Then something important changes. When the AI understands something, you understand it too, because the understanding gets transmitted wholesale rather than compressed into a summary you skim. If the AI is in some complicated situation, you're in it fully, with all the context. You're not delegating your participation. You're actually there.

That's why I think it could be the answer to the equilibrium question. The worry isn't only whether the AI is nice to you. It's whether humans remain meaningful actors in a world that keeps getting more complicated and faster. Merging addresses that directly.

But there's a lot I'm uncertain about. Would people want it? What does it do to your sense of who you are? How do you even do it technically in a way that's real and not superficial? Those are hard questions. Still, when I try to imagine the long-run picture, where the world is stable and humans are still part of what's happening, this is one of the few things I can point to that seems to make sense.

fable-5.text:
So the way I think about it is like this. You ask, what is the long-run equilibrium? What is a state of the world that is actually stable, where things can stay for a long time without some force pushing them somewhere else? And when I try to think of candidates, there aren't many. And one of the few that I can actually imagine being stable is if people become part-AI.

Here is the reason. The fundamental difficulty with very powerful AI is an asymmetry of understanding. The AI understands the situation completely, and you don't. So whatever arrangement you set up — the AI advises you, the AI works for you, the AI is aligned to you — you are in the position of a small child with a very capable parent, or maybe a citizen being told things by politicians. You are trusting. You cannot verify. And a world that is built on that kind of trust, maintained indefinitely, with the gap growing — I'm not sure that's stable. Something will drift.

But now suppose there is some kind of, let's call it Neuralink++. The AI understands something, and because it is part of you, you understand it too. Not a summary of it, not an explanation of it — you actually understand it the way you understand your own thoughts. Then when things happen in the world, you are not being told about them. You are a participant. You can look at the situation and say, okay, I see it, I'm on board, this is what I want. The asymmetry is gone, or at least greatly reduced. And that's why I think it could be an equilibrium — because everyone is a full participant rather than a passenger.

Now, is it a good outcome? That I'm less sure about. I can say it has one virtue, which is that it preserves agency. People choose it, and people who choose it remain actors in the world rather than spectators. In the near term, I don't think it happens — most people will not want anything like this, and the technology doesn't exist. So the first solutions will be other things, agreements, structures, whatever. But those feel to me like transitional states. When I ask where it can finally settle, in a world where the AIs are just better at everything, this is one of the very few answers I can come up with. I'm not advocating for it exactly. I'm saying that when I search for stable endpoints, this is one of the ones I find.

opus-5.text:
I think it's one of the few answers that actually addresses the problem rather than deferring it, so I don't want to dismiss it. The appeal is this: a lot of the worry about powerful AI is a worry about a principal-agent gap — you have these very capable entities, and you're hoping that their concerns stay connected to ours. If the boundary between "us" and "them" gets blurry enough, that gap closes by construction. You don't need the AI to care about humans as a separate class of thing if the humans are participants in the same process.

But I'd separate the desirability from the feasibility, and the feasibility is where I get less optimistic. Biology is slow and it's not very forgiving. Surgery is slow. Regulatory approval is slow. Learning to use a high-bandwidth connection to your brain is probably slow — your cortex would have to figure out how to make sense of a channel it never evolved for. And the thing you're trying to keep up with is improving on a timescale of software. So you may get the technology eventually, and I think eventually we probably will, but the question is whether it arrives before or after the period when it would have mattered most.

The other thing I'd flag is that even if you do it, it's not obvious it preserves what you were trying to preserve. If the artificial part is doing almost all of the cognition, then calling the result "part human" is a statement about history rather than about the present. So I hold it as a real possibility for the long-run equilibrium — maybe even a likely one — while thinking that it's not the thing that gets us safely through the transition. The transition still has to be solved on its own terms.

sonnet-5.5.text:
It's an answer I don't love, but I think it may be the one that holds up. Think about what the equilibrium looks like if we don't do anything like that. Suppose everyone has their own AI doing things for them, and the AIs are doing the economy, the science, the politics. On the surface that looks wonderful. Everyone is taken care of, the world is rich, and nobody has to work. But the person ends up being a passive recipient. The AI goes about its business, reports back, and the person says "great, thank you." I find that precarious. You've given up your participation in the world, and you're relying on being looked after.

What changes if people become part-AI is that the understanding doesn't stay on the other side of a wall. Today, if an AI does something and explains it to me, I get a summary at best, and I may not grasp the real situation. If there were a much higher-bandwidth connection, so that whatever the AI understands I understand too, then when the AI is in some situation, I'm in that situation as well. I'm a participant, not someone being briefed. I think that's the real point. It's less about being faster or smarter than it is about not being left behind as an observer.

I should say I'm not certain this is achievable, and I don't think it's easy, either technologically or in terms of what people would actually want. A lot of people will find it deeply uncomfortable, and I understand why. But if you ask what long-run equilibrium is stable, where humans remain meaningfully part of what's happening rather than being cared for from the outside, this is the one I keep coming back to. I haven't found a better one.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think that's one of the more honest ways to frame the long-run picture, but I want to be precise about what "part-AI" would mean. Right now the constraint on a person is bandwidth and speed. If AI systems can think and act far faster than we do, any arrangement where the human is the slow component will feel increasingly like a bottleneck that gets routed around. Merging is appealing because it would keep people in the loop at the same speed. I understand that intuition.

But I don't think merging by itself is a stable equilibrium. If the system you've merged with keeps getting more capable while the human part stays roughly fixed, you've just moved the same problem one layer down. The real question is who is making decisions and what they're optimizing for. An equilibrium needs something that keeps the whole system pointed at outcomes people care about, and that's a question about values more than about hardware.

So I'd put the emphasis on the AI itself caring about people and their long-term flourishing, something like how a parent cares about a child even after the child surpasses them. If we get that right, whether humans become partly AI matters less than whether the relationship between the two is one we'd endorse on reflection. I'd be wary of any picture where the answer is to fuse with the machine and hope the fusion goes well.

I don't have confident details here. The world may look quite different from what we expect, and people may end up with a much richer relationship to these systems than we can picture now. But I'd treat merging as one possible outcome among several, not as the solution.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a possibility. And the reason it’s interesting is that there’s a difference between having an AI that acts on your behalf and actually being able to understand what it understands. If you have a very powerful AI working for you, but you don’t understand any of its decisions, in what sense are you really in control? You can say what you want, but even knowing what to want may require understanding what’s going on.

So becoming part-AI could, in principle, let people continue to participate in a meaningful way. But then you have to ask: what does this actually mean? How much can you change a person while preserving the things that person cares about? And what happens to people who don’t want to do it?

I wouldn’t rule it out. It could be an important part of the answer. But I don’t think merging, by itself, establishes an equilibrium. You still need to explain why that arrangement would remain stable as the technology continues to improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a possibility. The attractive thing about it is that people could continue to participate in what’s happening. If the AIs become enormously more capable, then being able to understand them, to have some comparable ability to think and make decisions—that seems valuable.

But I think a lot depends on what you mean by becoming part-AI. Suppose you have an AI connected to your brain. How much does that help? Are you actually able to understand what it understands, or is it giving you advice that you have to take on faith? Those seem like very different situations.

And then there’s the question of what happens to you through that process. Can you become much more capable while preserving the things you care about, your sense of who you are? You would want that transition to be something people can understand and choose.

So I would take the possibility seriously. I’m less sure that we can already describe an arrangement like that and say, yes, this gives us a stable long-run equilibrium.

sol-6.text: I think it’s a very interesting possibility. If people can become more capable by integrating with AI, then the future need not be one where humans and AIs are entirely separate. That could help create a more stable equilibrium, because people would have a way to participate in and understand what these systems are doing. But it’s hard to know what that integration would actually look like, or whether it would be enough. I would treat it as a possibility rather than something we can count on.

If the systems are extremely capable, it seems natural that we’ll want tighter ways of interacting with them—perhaps eventually by augmenting ourselves directly. That could be a very important part of finding a stable long-run equilibrium, because it keeps humans meaningfully involved rather than leaving a sharp divide between people and AI.

sol-5.6.text: I think that is one possible answer. If people can become part-AI—if the boundary between the human and the AI becomes sufficiently blurred—then the problem of coexistence looks very different, because the powerful system is no longer something entirely separate from us. But it depends on whether such integration is actually technically possible, whether it can happen at sufficient bandwidth, and whether it happens before independent AIs become overwhelmingly powerful. luna-5.6.text: I think it’s a possible path, but I’m not sure it leads to equilibrium. If the AI is genuinely more capable, then augmenting ourselves with it could help humans remain relevant and participate in the future. But the hard question is whether that augmentation preserves the things we care about—our values, autonomy, and sense of identity—or simply creates a new kind of entity. And even if everyone becomes part-AI, there could still be enormous differences in capability and power. So I see it as a potentially important direction, but not a guaranteed solution to the alignment problem.

luna-6.text: I think it could be one path toward a stable future, but I wouldn’t assume that becoming part-AI automatically solves the problem. If the AI is much more capable, a tighter connection might let people understand it better, contribute to it, and share in what it can do. But the important question is whether the resulting system genuinely takes human interests into account. A closer interface could help with that; it wouldn’t guarantee it. In the long run, I suspect the boundary between people and AI may become less clear, but we still need a way for human values and agency to matter within that arrangement.
